title: The Wolf and the Horse
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Wolf on his rambles came to a field of oats, but, not being able to eat them, he was passing on his way when a Horse came along. "Look," said the Wolf, "here's a fine field of oats. For your sake I have left it untouched, and I shall greatly enjoy the sound of your teeth munching the ripe grain." But the Horse replied, "If wolves could eat oats, my fine friend, you would hardly have indulged your ears at the cost of your belly." There is no virtue in giving to others what is useless to oneself.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Wolf come to on his rambles?
options: A field of oats
A river full of fish
A pasture of sheep
An orchard of apple trees

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the Wolf pass on his way from the field?
options: He was not able to eat the oats
He heard a Horse approaching
He had already eaten his fill elsewhere
He was frightened by the farmer nearby

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Wolf claim he has done for the Horse's sake?
options: Left the field of oats untouched
Guarded the field from other animals
Told the farmer the field needed watering
Warned other wolves away from it

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Wolf say he will enjoy?
options: The sound of the Horse's teeth munching the ripe grain
Watching the Horse graze from a distance
Sharing the field equally with the Horse
The smell of the ripening oats

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Horse say the Wolf would have done if wolves could eat oats?
options: He would not have indulged his ears at the cost of his belly
He would have shared the field with the Horse
He would have eaten the oats long before the Horse arrived
He would have warned the farmer about the field

questions.prompt: According to the closing line, what is there no virtue in?
options: Giving to others what is useless to oneself
Trusting a wolf's kind words
Eating food that belongs to another
Passing by a field without stopping

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Horse doubt the Wolf's claim of generosity?
options: He recognizes that the Wolf left the oats untouched only because he could not eat them anyway
He believes the Wolf secretly wants to eat the oats himself later
He thinks the Wolf is lying about ever finding the field at all
He suspects the farmer told the Wolf to guard the field

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: A gift that costs the giver nothing is no real proof of kindness
Wolves and horses can never truly be friends
Fields of oats are more valuable to horses than to wolves
Flattery always succeeds in winning over its target

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who approached the Wolf as he was leaving the field?
options: A Horse
A Sheep
A Farmer
Another Wolf

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Wolf describe the field to the Horse?
options: As a fine field of oats
As a small and poor field
As a field belonging to a farmer he knows
As a field he had guarded for weeks

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Horse call the Wolf when he answers him?
options: My fine friend
My old enemy
Sir Wolf
Neighbour

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the phrase "indulged your ears at the cost of your belly" imply about what the Wolf would have done if he could eat oats?
options: He would have eaten the oats himself rather than merely praising them to the Horse
He would have listened to the Horse eat rather than joining in
He would have shared the sound of eating with the Horse equally
He would have refused to speak of the oats at all

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "rambles" mean in "on his rambles"?
options: Wanderings without a fixed destination
Fierce battles with rivals
Long periods of sleep
Formal visits to other animals

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Wolf who cannot eat a field of oats pretends generosity toward a Horse, but the Horse sees the offer for what it is
A Wolf and Horse share a field of oats without any disagreement
A Horse steals oats from a field the Wolf was guarding
A Wolf tricks a Horse into leaving a field so he can eat the oats himself
